title: Mathematics & Technology
subtitle: The real mathematics, statistics, algorithms and physics behind Lotto Simulator — taken from the code that runs in the app.
html:
How to read this page

Every formula below is copied from the implementation, not from a brochure. Where a component is a deterministic rule or a heuristic rather than a formula, we describe the algorithm exactly as it runs and do not invent mathematics for it.

Lotto Simulator is an analytical, educational and simulation environment. It generates combinations with sixteen methods, reviews them in a Mathematical Court of twelve jurors, six defence counsel and a Supreme Judge, tests real draw histories for fairness, analyses calendar coincidences and replays a physical 3D lottery drum. None of this changes the probability of any number in an official draw — section 8 explains why, with the numbers.

Notation used throughout

In plain words Each draw contributes exactly main numbers, so the counts always add up to , and the expected count of any number in a fair lottery is .

1. System architecture

One application, one code base: the same web app runs in desktop and mobile browsers and, unchanged, inside the iOS and Android apps (Capacitor WebView). Heavy and paid computation runs on the server; everything the user sees is rendered on the device.

  1. Device (web, iOS, Android)Interface, ticket and working sets, the four FREE generator methods, frequency charts, χ² test, calendar maths, 3D drum. Pure random and the 3D drum take their randomness from the Web Crypto API.
  2. Edge functions (TypeScript, Deno)The twelve PRO generator methods, all nineteen Court models, the twelve jurors, six counsel, the Supreme Judge, wheel designs, the prediction ledger. The Court runs on seeded, reproducible random streams.
  3. Database (PostgreSQL)Official draw results with their rule version, payout tables, accounts and entitlements, the append-only prediction ledger and its evaluation.
  4. Data pipelineScheduled jobs collect official results, validate every draw against the rules of its era and publish the current-rules data set.

Who computes what

  • In the browser: the FREE methods (Hot numbers, Combined, Segment coverage, Pure random) and all descriptive statistics. The public build physically removes the PRO implementations from the client: their functions are replaced by stubs, so a PRO result can only come from the server.
  • On the server: every PRO method, the whole Mathematical Court and the Supreme Judge. A request carries the lottery, the method, the number of rows (1–50) and the analysis window; the server loads the draws itself, so the client cannot feed it invented history.
  • Fail-closed rule: a server model needs at least 5 draws in the selected analysis window. With fewer it refuses with an explicit "insufficient history" answer instead of producing rows from nothing.

Reproducible Court computation

Every juror, counsel and model inside the Court runs on its own pseudo-random stream whose seed is a hash of the algorithm version, the persona, the lottery, the complete draw history and the target draw date. The same data therefore always produces the same verdict, and any change to the history changes every stream.

where
algorithm version of the Court engine
persona or model key, for example a juror's identifier
every draw of the window, main and bonus numbers in order
lottery identifier and target draw date
the FNV-1a offset basis; hashes the text starting from the state
the -th uniform random number of the stream
In plain words Generators that produce rows for you use cryptographic randomness and are deliberately not reproducible; the Court is deliberately reproducible so that a verdict can be audited.

Persistence and provenance

Every combination carries a provenance record: its source (generator method, juror, jury consensus, wheel, 3D draw, Supreme Judge, manual entry), the numbers it started with and an append-only event log of reviews, proposals, counsel positions, verdicts, decisions and transformations (at most 200 events). A record is accepted only if replaying its transformations on the initial numbers reproduces the row exactly; otherwise the row is shown as having an unavailable source.

  • Lineage: when a row is edited by hand, a new record is created whose parent is the previous one (up to four earlier records are kept), so the history before the manual change remains visible.
  • Prediction ledger: every recommendation (a generated row, a juror's replacement, a counsel's position, a verdict) is written to a ledger before the target draw and evaluated automatically after the official result.

2. Main generator: sixteen methods

The generator offers sixteen selections. Four FREE methods run in the browser; twelve PRO methods run on the server. All of them pick distinct numbers from plus the bonus numbers of the lottery; they differ only in how numbers are weighted or constructed.

Shared building blocks

Weighted methods assign a weight to every number and then draw sequentially without replacement: each pick removes the number and renormalises the remaining weights.

where
the -th number picked for the row,
the method's weight of number
In plain words Only the first pick follows the weights exactly; later picks are renormalised over the numbers still available. A uniform pick is the special case .

Randomness: in the browser, Pure random and the uniqueness step use the Web Crypto API, while Hot numbers, Combined and Segment coverage use the browser's standard generator (Math.random). On the server the methods draw from cryptographic randomness, except the Physical model (standard generator) and the Chaos seed, which mixes cryptographic randomness with a high-resolution timer. In the browser an unbiased integer in is obtained by rejection sampling, so no residue is favoured:

Bonus numbers

Bonus numbers (Eurojackpot 2 of 12, EuroMillions 2 of 12, Powerball 1 of 26, Mega Ball 1 of 24, Viking number 1 of 5, Powerball AU 1 of 20) are drawn from their own pool, independently of the main numbers. Lotto, SuperEnalotto and Lotto Max have no bonus number for the player: their extra ball is drawn by the operator from the main drum.

FREE filters and uniqueness

Rows produced in the browser pass three filters that are switched on by default: not all numbers even or all odd; the sum inside a range; no run of more than three consecutive numbers. A rejected row is replaced by a uniformly random row that passes the filters (its bonus numbers are drawn with the Bayes weights ).

To avoid handing out the same combination twice on the same device, each FREE row is identified by the lexicographic rank of its main numbers among all combinations and compared with the last 20 000 rows issued for that lottery; a repeated rank is altered by random swaps, and as a last resort the next unused rank is taken from a random affine permutation of all ranks. A row altered in this way is not checked against the filters again.

Limitations A plug-in frequency estimate with almost no smoothing: a number never seen keeps only weight 0.05. In independent draws past frequency carries no predictive information.

Combined

FREEIn the browser

Purpose: mix hot, medium and cold numbers in a fixed proportion.

Numbers are sorted by (ties keep the smaller number first) and split into thirds of size : hot, middle, cold. Row takes uniform picks from each third:

Advanced details
Example Eurojackpot : 2 hot numbers, then 2 middle and 1 cold, or 1 middle and 2 cold, alternating between rows. Lotto : 3 hot, 2 middle, 2 cold.
Limitations The tercile is the only information used; the proportion is a design choice, not a statistical estimate.

Segment coverage

FREEIn the browser

Purpose: spread a row evenly across the number range.

Advanced details
Example Lotto 7/34: , segments 1–4, 5–8, …, 21–24 and the wider last segment 25–34. A number in the last segment is therefore chosen with probability , the others with .
Limitations History is not used. Every combination produced has exactly one number per segment, so most combinations of the lottery can never appear.

Pure random

FREEIn the browser

Purpose: the honest baseline — every number equally likely.

Advanced details
Limitations In the browser the default filters remove all-even/all-odd rows, out-of-range sums and long runs, so the rows shown are uniform only over the combinations that pass the filters.

Wheel matrix

PROServer

Purpose: build several rows that together cover as many pairs of a small number pool as possible — a greedy covering design.

The pool has numbers taken alternately from the hot, cold and middle thirds. All combinations of the pool are candidates (above 40 000 a random sample is used); each step adds the candidate with the best score and marks its pairs as covered:

Advanced details
where

Example Eurojackpot: pool of 10 numbers, candidates and pairs; each row covers pairs. Every number must meet 9 partners and a row gives it only 4, so each number needs at least 3 rows: at least rows are needed to cover every pair.
Limitations The server optimises pair coverage (t = 2). It does not prove a minimum number of rows and gives no prize guarantee.

World hot and World combined

PROServer

Purpose: transfer the frequency profile of all nine supported lotteries onto the current one.

Each drawn number of every lottery is mapped to its relative position and spread with a narrow Gaussian kernel onto the numbers of the current lottery; every lottery gets the same weight per draw, and the current lottery's own frequency is added once more on top:

Advanced details
  • World hot: uniform picks from the numbers with the highest score.
  • World combined: from the top third, from the bottom third, the rest from the middle. Bonus numbers are uniform.
Limitations Lotteries are physically independent; a "resonance" between relative positions in different games has no causal meaning.

Markov chains

PROServer

Purpose: weight numbers by how often they followed the numbers of the previous draw.

Advanced details
where

In plain words Because every row of transition probabilities sums to one, .
Example Eurojackpot: if each of the 5 latest numbers was followed 50 times and followed them 3, 2, 2, 1 and 2 times, then , against the uniform .
Limitations For independent draws the transition counts are just products of marginal frequencies plus noise.

Gauss · central limit theorem

PROServer

Purpose: build rows whose sum is typical. The sum of numbers drawn without replacement has

Advanced details

Each number is weighted by a Gaussian around the average value per position, and up to 40 candidate rows are drawn; the one whose sum is closest to wins (the search stops early within ):

Example Eurojackpot prior: , , , centred on 25.5.
Limitations A typical sum says nothing about the chance of a particular row: every combination, typical or not, has the same probability.

Interval model Δ

PROServer

Purpose: imitate the spacing between neighbouring numbers in real draws.

From the latest 120 draws it collects the smallest number of each draw and all differences between neighbouring sorted numbers. A row is built as a random start plus random differences; a row that runs past is rejected (up to 300 tries, then a uniform row):

Advanced details
Limitations Rejecting rows that overshoot under-represents the highest numbers. For this reason the Court does not use Δ as a juror source.

PROServer

Purpose: frequency with shrinkage towards uniform.

Advanced details
Example Eurojackpot : a number seen 6 times gets , against for uniform; one never seen gets .
Limitations With long histories the prior is negligible and the method converges to Hot numbers.

Gap analysis

PROServer

Purpose: favour numbers that have not appeared for a long time.

Advanced details
Example Eurojackpot, : gap 0 → 0.15; gap 10 → 1.15; gap 25 → 4.48; gap 40 → 9.34.
Limitations This is the gambler's fallacy turned into a weight: the method shows gaps, it does not change any ball's chance.

Physical model of the drum

PROServer

Purpose: let a simplified 2D simulation decide the order of exit.

discs of radius move in a unit square with random air gusts, a constant drift towards the outlet, damping and elastic collisions of equal masses; a disc leaving through the outlet in the middle of the bottom wall is drawn.

Advanced details
Limitations Only up to 18 random pairs are tested for collision per step. This is not the 3D drum of section 4, and it does not use history.

PROServer

Purpose: demonstrate that a fully deterministic system can be unpredictable.

Advanced details
In plain words Near the map's invariant density is close to , which piles up at both ends of the interval.
Example Eurojackpot: under that density the first bin gets probability , about 4.5 times the uniform . Numbers 1 and 50 are therefore strongly over-represented — an artefact, not data.

Purpose: a contrarian weight that favours rarely drawn numbers.

Example Eurojackpot , : , , .
Limitations The name is figurative: the entropy is the platform's cryptographic generator, not a quantum device.

System of paradoxes

PROServerExperimental

Purpose: research rows built on counter-intuitive properties of random combinations. Five archetypes are used in turn:

  • Crowd: prefers numbers above 31 in pools of at least 42 numbers (birthdays end at 31), weight 2.6 above the cut and 0.28 below, ×1.1 for multiples of 10, then forces at least numbers above the cut. Fewer people play such numbers, so a win would be shared less — the chance of winning is unchanged.
  • Clash: half of the row from the most frequent numbers, the rest from the longest-absent ones.
  • Cluster: contains a pair of consecutive numbers — a property far more common in random draws than intuition suggests:
Advanced details
  • Mirror: pairs and .
  • Regression: the numbers whose recent rate (last 10 draws) differs most from their long-run rate.
Limitations Experimental research mode. Every archetype is a construction rule, not a probability advantage.

3. The Mathematical Court

The Court reviews a combination you already have. Jurors and models may propose replacing one number; defence counsel argue for or against each proposal; the Supreme Judge rules on a structural field of past draws. Numbers change only when you decide — and every step is recorded.

The order of a case

  • Proposal. A juror or a model scans every possible single swap of the row and proposes at most one replacement — or proposes to keep the row.
  • Defence. Counsel take a position on each proposal: support, objection or protest. A counsel never proposes or applies a number.
  • Verdict. The Supreme Judge accepts the proposal, offers an alternative or keeps the number, using the structural field of past draws.
  • Decision. Only you change numbers: accept a proposal, follow the defence, accept the Judge, keep the original or revert. Each decision is stored with its author.

From a model to a per-number preference

Every model is reduced to a relative preference for each number, where 1 means "the model's average", together with a standard error. Models defined by an explicit weight vector are exact; the others are measured by running them:

In plain words The value 1.0 is exactly what a uniform model would give: is the chance that a given number appears in a uniform row.

The nineteen models

The Court uses the sixteen generator methods of section 2 plus three Court models. Four of them use no history and are registered as having no number preference (Segment coverage, Pure random, Physical model, Chaos); in practice Segment coverage favours the numbers of short segments when does not divide , and Chaos favours the edges of the range, as their cards show. Two models are composites (Consensus and Structural field).

How a model reviews a row

For each possible swap — number leaves the row, number enters — the model computes the gain and its noise. A gain counts only if it is statistically clear; a loss always counts.

In plain words Scanning 225 swaps of a Eurojackpot row and taking the best would turn noise into "evidence". The correction keeps the error rate of the whole scan at the level of a single test.

Signals computed from history

Three jurors use signals read directly from the draws rather than from a generator. With :

Structural components compare a row with the profile of past draws: parity, low/high, clusters and gaps are categorical with Laplace smoothing; sum and spread are Gaussian.

Strategy: long-run frequency with Bayesian shrinkage. Sources: Bayes 0.8 + Hot numbers 0.2; ; ; no significance test (exact weights).

The Supreme Judge

The Judge rules on a disputed number using the structural field , normalised to its maximum: . A number is weak if it lies in the lowest 35% of the field.

Example Normalised field: current 0.50, threshold 0.55, proposal 0.56, best alternative 0.95. Without protests → accept the proposal. If two of three counsel protest, the bar is → alternative 0.95. A current number at 0.70 is kept whatever the jury voted.
In plain words Jury votes never move the verdict; they are only reported as agreement or disagreement. The defence can only raise the bar.

Supreme Judge analysis and recommendation

For whole rows the Judge reports a row score and suggests replacing up to of the weakest numbers below by the strongest numbers outside the row. You choose which swaps to apply. With no rows, the Judge recommends: uniform random drafts are improved in the same way and returned with their provenance.

Decisions, batches and history

  • Decisions: accept the proposal, accept the defence, accept the Judge, keep the original, revert. Numbers change only when you accept a proposal, accept a Judge verdict that replaces the number, or revert; each change is a transformation in the provenance record.
  • Bulk decisions: at most one replacement per number. "Accept all majority replacements" applies only options chosen by more than half of the selected jurors; "Apply all proposals" takes, for each number, the majority option or else the one with the most votes, and skips ties.
  • Batches: a review of up to 50 rows by the same line-up of personas counts as one attempt; rows already analysed are skipped and an interrupted batch resumes with the same plan.
  • History: event types are jury review, model review, proposal, defence review, Judge review, decision and transformation; the log keeps up to 200 events and never drops a transformation or the latest reviews.

Holding the Court to account

Every claim is written to the prediction ledger before its draw and scored afterwards against chance. For claims about numbers with base chance :

In plain words Numbers inside one draw are drawn without replacement, so the exact variance of a claim of numbers is ; claims about the same draw are also summed as if independent. The ranking's is therefore an approximation. A lift near 1 is what chance predicts for every method.

4. The 3D drum: physics engine

The 3D draw is a real-time rigid-body simulation: balls are bodies with mass, inertia, friction and restitution, pushed by gravity, a stirring rotor and an air field, and the drawn ball is the one that physically falls through the outlet. It is a credible physical model of a drum, not a recording of a real machine.

Engine and coordinates

Physics runs in Rapier 3D (version 0.14, WebAssembly); rendering uses Three.js (r169). The world is right-handed with up and the origin at the centre of the chamber; the rotor axis is the horizontal axis and points towards the viewer.

  • Chamber: a sphere of radius units, built as a triangle mesh with inward normals and a circular outlet at the bottom (half-angle ).
  • Balls: spheres of radius and density 1; one ball per number, from 5 to 90 balls.
  • Rotor: a kinematic shaft with six arms whose capsule paddles are sized to stop 0.14 units from the glass in their plane of rotation, plus a smaller three-arm rotor whose direction alternates between mix phases.
  • Gate: a cylindrical plug in the outlet, removed when a ball may leave.

Scale and Froude similarity

One model unit is 10 cm: a 40 mm ball is 0.4 units and the chamber is a 600 mm sphere. Gravity is reduced to units/s² instead of the real . Motion dominated by gravity and inertia looks the same when the Froude number is the same, so the simulation corresponds to a real-size machine with a slower clock:

In plain words The design rule stated in the configuration is that drag, suction and every rate must be expressed in this same scaled base. A physics regression test checks the length unit and the ball mass; the other rates follow the configuration.

Forces

Every ball obeys Newton's second law with the forces that the code actually applies:

Air field and quadratic drag

The blower is modelled as a prescribed air-velocity field ; each ball feels quadratic drag towards the local air velocity. The drag constant is fixed by a terminal speed of 48 units/s:

  • Swirl: a horizontal rotation of 11 units/s about the vertical axis.
  • Inward flow: beyond 60% of the radius, up to towards the centre, so balls keep cycling instead of hugging the glass.
  • Turbulence: smooth three-dimensional value noise of amplitude 58 that drifts in time; it is a fixed deterministic function, not a random number generator.
  • Anti-stall gusts: a ball that stays too long at the bottom, at the top, at the wall or almost motionless gets a local gust added to the air velocity, still acting through drag.

Analytic spherical wall

On top of the mesh, the glass is enforced as an exact sphere at the velocity level, which prevents tunnelling and gives correct rolling. With outward normal , outward speed and penetration :

In plain words Why : an impulse at the surface of a solid sphere changes the contact-point velocity by , so stopping the slip completely costs . That is exactly the condition for rolling without slipping.

Contacts between bodies

Ball–ball, ball–rotor and ball–gate contacts are solved by Rapier's constraint solver with continuous collision detection on the balls. Coefficients are combined by averaging:

Damping is small during the draw (linear 0.05, angular 0.035) and strong while balls settle (2.4). There is no rolling resistance parameter: rolling slows only through damping and contact friction.

Time stepping and integration

The simulation advances in fixed steps independent of the screen refresh rate; each frame runs as many fixed steps as real time requires, at most five:

Within a sub-step the engine updates velocities from forces and then positions from the new velocities — the semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler scheme used by impulse-based engines, shown here as the general principle:

The application's own forces (air, wall, suction) are computed once per step from the state at its start and held over both sub-steps. The rotor is kinematic and is re-targeted every sub-step:

How a ball is selected

After 1 s of start-up and 2.6 s of mixing the gate opens. While the outlet is open the updraft above it collapses smoothly, the central jet is reduced to 62% and a suction of about 2.2 ball weights (about 4 after 5 s) pulls balls near the outlet:

The drawn ball is the first one whose centre falls below ; if several do in the same step, the lowest. No random number is consulted at that moment. The random numbers of a draw are the initial placement of the balls and a small initial velocity and spin, taken from the Web Crypto API (again when a separate bonus pool is loaded). The ball then travels along the exit path to the rack; that motion is scripted, not simulated.

Rendering versus simulation versus randomness

  • Simulation: fixed 1/60 s steps; quality presets (ultra, high, medium, low) change shadows, bloom, resolution and mesh detail only, never the physics.
  • Rendering: each frame shows the last completed step; there is no interpolation between steps.
  • Randomness: the forces are deterministic; the outcome depends on the initial placement and, from the second ball on, also on how long the reveal of the previous ball takes on the device, so a draw cannot be replayed exactly.
Limitations Not simulated: the chamber does not rotate; the air is a prescribed field, not computational fluid dynamics (no pressure, no wakes, no Magnus effect); every ball has identical mass and size; the exit tube and rack have no colliders. The simulated drum does not reproduce the trajectories or results of any real lottery machine, and official draws are independent of it.

5. Statistics of real draws

The analytics screens describe historical draws. They answer "what happened" and "is this consistent with a fair lottery", never "what will happen".

Frequencies, hot and cold

For each number the app counts appearances in the window and shows them next to the expected count of a fair lottery; the standard deviation is given here for reference:

  • Hot and cold: the five most and least frequent numbers, each with its expected count (at least 5 draws are required).
  • Frequency bars: red when a number's share exceeds 1.3 times the expected share, blue below 0.7 times.
  • Heat map: colour by min–max normalisation .
Example Eurojackpot, : and . A count of 6 is less than two standard deviations above expectation — and among 50 numbers several such counts are normal.

Fairness test: χ² with a correction

The χ² test checks whether the counts are consistent with equal probabilities. In one draw the numbers are taken without replacement, which makes counts negatively correlated; the plain multinomial statistic is then too small, and the app corrects it:

Positional Q-test

With at least 30 complete draws the app also tests the average of each sorted position (Coronel-Brizio et al., arXiv:0806.4595). The -th smallest of numbers drawn from has mean and covariance

Example Eurojackpot: the expected sorted positions are 8.5, 17, 25.5, 34 and 42.5.
Limitations Both tests can only detect a deviation; passing them does not make any number more or less likely, and with short windows their power is low.

Pairs, comparisons and checks

  • Pairs: a 12 × 12 matrix of how often the 12 most frequent numbers appeared together (at least 10 draws). These are raw counts; for reference, the expected count of a given pair in fair draws is .
  • Comparison of lotteries: jackpot odds, price, the cost of buying every combination.
  • Mathematics check: the app recomputes and compares it with the stored constant, and checks the draws of the analysis window for range errors, wrong ball counts and duplicate dates.
  • Prize tiers: official payout tables per draw. The draw picture averages the last 60 real payout tables; only for a lottery with no payout data at all does it estimate winners from the tier probabilities of section 8 and an assumed sales volume, so those figures are illustrative.

6. Calendar analysis

Calendar analysis looks for coincidences between draw dates and drawn numbers — for example the day of the month appearing among the balls — and compares each observed rate with the rate that pure chance would produce.

Selecting draws

Draws can be filtered by year, month, the same month across all years or a date range, and by rule era. Frequency lists (hot, cold, longest absent) use raw counts in the selection; a number that is impossible in every selected era is left out, and a selection that mixes eras is flagged with a warning, because a number valid only in the newer era looks falsely "cold". The date rules below are era-aware: a draw counts for a rule only if at least one candidate is a valid number of that draw's own rules.

Interpreting the rates

Limitations A coincidence is an observation about a past draw, not a sign of higher probability. The analysis compares past counts with your rows, but it does not compute an expected number of matches for them. FREE runs it without limits on the recent FREE window; PRO adds the full archive.

Why no method can beat chance

If draws are independent and every combination is equally likely, the conditional probability of the next draw given any history is the same as without it, and the expected number of matched main numbers is the same for every row, however it was produced:

In plain words The law of large numbers says that frequencies approach over very many draws; it does not say that a number which has been "cold" must catch up. Deviations are diluted, not compensated.
